title: Joy is allowed
hookLine: the Stoics kept joy among their good feelings; Psalm 30 sings mourning turned to dancing
tomorrow: how did Thoreau spend a whole summer morning doing nothing?

cards: Someone posts good news in the group chat, and the first reply is: must be nice. Even in a happy moment, a small voice can say: careful, don't enjoy this too much. The Stoics are well-known for distrusting feelings.

Fear, craving, wild excitement: they called them passions, and they wanted to be free of them. But they kept a short list of good feelings, steady ones that come from a sound mind. And one of them was joy.

teach.b: Seneca writes to his friend Lucilius, and his advice sounds surprising from a Stoic: "Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy." He means a deep joy, not a thrill.
Joy that grows from inside, from living well, so a bad day can't take it. The Stoics even had a name for this steady joy, chara, and set it apart from the passions they distrusted.
So today's question: is joy allowed when things are still hard? The Stoic answer: yes, the right kind, rooted in how you live, and it can be learned. Now a neighbor, in its own words.
Psalm 30, prayed by Jews and Christians, has joy that arrives through hardship.
It says, in the King James Version: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." And then: "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing."
What's shared: both treat joy as serious, not a guilty extra, and both say it can come after pain. The honest difference: Seneca's joy grows from within, from your own virtue.
The psalm's joy is a gift, turned for the singer by God.

how: Stoic writers kept joy (chara) among the 'good feelings' of a sound mind; Seneca's 23rd letter urges Lucilius to learn how to feel joy. Jews and Christians pray Psalm 30, which turns mourning into dancing.

o: joy is fine to feel, even while life is still hard
joy should wait until every trouble is fully over
joy is a reward handed out for being good enough

games.q: joy, two ways: tap the pairs.
p: the Stoics' word for good joy

s: the Stoics tried to have no feelings at all
they kept a short list of good feelings, and joy was one.
Seneca told Lucilius to learn how to feel joy
"Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy."
Psalm 30 says joy is for those who never weep
"weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."

games.q: your cousin's wedding is a month after your grandmother's funeral. your aunt says dancing would be disrespectful. what fits both Seneca and Psalm 30?
o: joy can come after grief without erasing it; dancing is allowed.
skip the dancing; real joy should wait until the grief is gone.
dance, but only for show, so nobody thinks the family is sad.
games.why: Seneca says learn joy; the psalm says mourning can be turned into dancing. neither makes joy wait for every sorrow to end.

practice: Put on one piece of music that lifts you, or listen to the happiest sound near you: a bird, kids laughing down the street, a kettle starting to sing. Let it be good, all the way through, without checking whether you've earned it.

wordCard.voice: Joy is allowed: the Stoics kept joy among their good feelings, and the psalm sings it after a night of weeping.
